explanation: Traditional Italian and Spanish packs have a suit of swords beside coins and batons. English borrowed spade, Italian for swords, for the French suit, so the garden tool has nothing to do with it.

claims.text: The name of the spades suit comes from Italian spade (swords), or the related Spanish espadas.
The names clubs, hearts and diamonds do not come from a word for sword.
Traditional Italian and Spanish packs use the suits swords, cups, coins and batons (clubs).
The suit name spade for playing cards is unrelated to the digging tool called a spade.

writerNotes: Subtopic: card games (thin in the pool, one or two items). lint: clean. claims: four; three high for etymology. datasets: none covers word origins; c1 and c4 need web evidence (a dictionary such as the OED, Merriam-Webster or Etymonline). rivalTest: the other three suits are the only possible options; clubs is the tempting one because Latin suits include clubs (bastoni), but 'club' is an English word for a cudgel, not a sword. Argued against the key: 'spade' the tool and 'spade' the suit look like one word, which is the surprise; dictionaries give them separate entries, the suit from Italian spade, plural of spada. The shape of the pip (a pike head in French packs) is a separate story that the item does not touch. volatility: evergreen. regional: the four-suit pack is used worldwide. style: Oxford spelling, explanation of 34 words (I left the cups suit out of the explanation because lint C21 reads 'cups' as a unit). myths: screened. mystery and encore: not applicable. doubts: c4 is the claim to watch: some sources say the English tool word and the Italian word share a distant Greek root (spathe). The item only says the suit is not named after the tool, which holds either way; if a checker objects, c4 and the last clause of the explanation can go.
stem: Which suit in a standard pack of playing cards takes its name from an Italian or Spanish word for 'sword'?

evidence.restatement: English spade for the suit comes from Italian spade, plural of spada meaning sword, with Spanish espada the sister word.

claimResults.note: Rival test: clubs derives from the Spanish baston (batons) suit sign, hearts and diamonds are plain English words. A search gave Wiktionary and etymology references for Italian spada via Latin spatha; the summary named its sources only as a group, so it is not cited. Memo 18 applies (both checks confirm directly).

evidence.restatement: Hearts, diamonds and clubs are not named after any sword word; clubs is the English word for the baton-like stick.
Italian and Spanish decks have swords, cups, coins and batons, the batons being what English calls clubs in translation.
The card suit and the digging tool share a spelling by coincidence, with different roots (Greek spathe versus Germanic).

claimResults.note: The dictionary entries in the search agree.

issues.note: Sources differ on whether Spanish espada was an intermediary; the stem's 'Italian or Spanish' and the claim's 'or the related' phrasing cover both, so the key holds either way.
